title: Stars Between the Strings
subtitle: Stars Between the Strings · Chapter 40 of 40
content:
The blanket had a new patch.

I noticed it when Greg spread it across the grass above the Beach City overlook. The patch was bright yellow and shaped like a star that had lost an argument with a pair of scissors.

"Did you sew that?" I asked.

"Don't look so shocked. I contain hidden talents."

"It's crooked."

"It's artistic."

He looked proud enough that I let the matter rest.

The sky was clearing. We had driven up after a long day of errands, bringing two sandwiches, a thermos, and the small notebook of unfinished songs Greg always claimed he was going to organize.

I sat where I could see the water.

"Different stars tonight," I said.

"Different from what?"

"Lanternweald. The sky changes when you cross a Threadway. Some of the constellations aren't even in the same places."

Greg leaned back on his elbows.

"You miss it?"

"Sometimes. Sometimes I miss this place when I'm there."

He was quiet.

I could tell the question he was trying not to ask: which home mattered more.

"You can ask," I said.

He looked at me.

"Ask what?"

"Whatever you're rehearsing in your head."

He laughed without much humor.

"That obvious?"

"Only to somebody who knows you."

He lay back on the blanket.

"I guess I wonder whether I'm one of the places you stop or one of the places you come home to."

I felt my chest tighten.

"We've talked about this."

"I know. Doesn't mean the worry never comes back."

I considered. He hadn't asked me to change my relationships, or to promise I would never leave. He'd told me something uncomfortable without turning it into a demand.

"You're one of the people I choose," I said. "Not a stop on a route."

He turned toward me.

"And the others?"

"I choose them too. I'm ethically non-monogamous, and I prefer polyamory. I didn't tell you that as a warning that our relationship would be less real. I told you because I wanted you to decide whether it was something you could freely be part of."

"I did decide."

"Yes."

He smiled faintly.

"I still get jealous sometimes."

"Then tell me when it happens. We can talk without making anybody a villain."

He looked up at the stars again.

"Okay."

We ate the sandwiches. Greg had packed mine with the right filling and his with twice as much mustard as any human needed. When I pointed it out, he insisted that mustard was a form of optimism.

I laughed so hard I nearly dropped the thermos.

After dinner he took out the notebook.

"Want to hear something?"

"Always."

He played a small melody he'd been working on, no more than a few measures. The notes moved like a road that bent out of sight and returned in an unexpected place. He stopped before the final phrase.

"That's where I'm stuck."

"Why?"

"I keep wanting to end it on the same note it began with."

"Would that be wrong?"

"No. Just predictable."

I looked at the blank lines in his notebook.

"Can the next part be different without ruining the first?"

He considered, then played the tune again, changing one chord.

I hummed a harmony that wasn't quite right.

Greg laughed.

"That note is absolutely not in the key."

"I know."

"Keep it."

"Why?"

"It makes the next one interesting."

We tried it again. This time the wrong note led somewhere we hadn't expected. He scribbled it down before forgetting.

For a while, we were two people making something, not trying to negotiate the entire future.

Then I remembered the small motel card he'd kept in the glovebox when we first met, the one with the phone number he'd been too nervous to call. I asked whether he still had it.

He searched the notebook.

"Why would it be in here?"

"Because you put everything important in the wrong place."

He pulled it from behind the page of song drafts.

I stared.

"Unbelievable."

"Organized chaos," he said.

The edges were worn. The number was almost illegible now.

"Do you remember why you kept it?" I asked.

"Because I was afraid I'd call and you'd say no."

"And now?"

"Now I know a no doesn't erase every yes we've had."

I looked at him.

"That's a difficult thing to learn."

"Tell me about it."

The wind picked up. Greg pulled the patched blanket around us.

I let myself rest against his shoulder. His hand settled over mine, warm and loose enough that I could move if I wanted.

"May I kiss you?" I asked.

He smiled.

"I'd be offended if you didn't."

"That's not quite an answer."

"Yes, Jasper."

I kissed him slowly. He tasted like mustard and tea, which was a strange combination, and we both laughed when I told him.

"That's romance," he said.

"That's a sandwich."

He kissed me again.

We stayed on the hill until the stars brightened and the town lights below looked like a second sky. We didn't have to name every future journey. We knew the ones already planned: Greg had a performance to prepare; I had a meeting at Moonroot; we wanted another day together before the next tide schedule changed.

He asked whether I'd like to stay at his place that night.

"Yes," I said.

We packed the blanket and carried the thermos back to the van. Later we closed the door, keeping the tender part of the night for ourselves.

In the morning Greg made breakfast with the last of the bread. I updated the calendar on his kitchen wall, making sure our next date was written where we'd both remember it.

He saw the entry and smiled.

"You're coming back."

"I said I would."

"I know." He put down the knife. "It's just nice to see it written."

I took his hand.

"Then we'll keep writing it when we choose."

Outside, the day began in Beach City. Beyond the Threadway, other places would begin their mornings at different hours, with their own weather, music, work and people.

I wasn't asking one town to hold my whole life.

I was asking each person I loved to let me arrive honestly and leave honestly, and to give them the same freedom.

Greg put the finished melody on the music stand.

He hadn't written a grand final chord.

I liked it better that way.

bridge_outro: By the next festival, Starwake Pier had become a place people crossed to hear one another. Greg played a set with room for mistakes, interruptions, and a very enthusiastic audience of one when Aang arrived with a borrowed flute. Iroh brought tea; Danse replaced a loose railing; Toph complained about the tempo while tapping her foot to it. Greg smiled at me over the strings, not asking whether he would be remembered forever. I walked beside him when the lights went out and helped fold the chairs. The Lanternweald was not the only home we had. It was the one where all those separate roads had begun to recognize each other.
